div.p: εις την ὐγέιαν σας και πόλλα χρόνια !

div.note: This item is a calling card imprinted “MR JAMES JOYCE” with the “MR” crossed out.

note.p: Gk. literal translation: “To your health and many years!” Our rendering of JJ’s text, written on a calling card, is a Unicode transcription (courtesy of Benjamin Keim, Department of Classics, Pomona College). JJ offers Pound (1885-1972) a typical Greek birthday wish, in the manner of a toast, for many happy returns of the day. Pound’s birthday was 30 October. He turned 38 on that day in 1923. JJ’s Greek may contain an error that renders his greeting literally “to the good health of you [plural] and many years” (courtesy of Stephanie Nelson). But it is possible that JJ was referring also to Pound’s wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), who had turned 37 on 14 September.

JJ’s use of Greek diacritical marks is spotty. Following classical (though not modern) Greek conventions, one might expect a smooth breathing (εἰς) above the first word and a rough breathing (ὑγείαν) above the third word. There is a noticeable mark above the second word that cannot be conveyed in Unicode; it is no more than a dot and thus neither an acute (used on three occasions, albeit on the wrong vowel of the diphthong – εί – of ὑγείαν) nor a grave (not used, though there should be one [τὴν, καὶ] over the second and fifth words). The final exclamation mark is, apparently, an acceptable modern (but not ancient) Greek mark of punctuation, and its usage parallels that of English.

As for the vocabulary and expressions, these are more or less modern Greek. A search of the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae database (focusing on 8th-3rd centuries B.C.) revealed no matches for the two major parts of JJ’s greeting. The possessive σας is definitely a modern form.
So, read through modern Greek lenses, Joyce gets marked off for his diacritical marks and receives more or less full marks for vocabulary.

It is possible that JJ’s “πόλλα κρόνια” is a mistake for “πόλλα χρόνια,” which literally means “many years.” It is easy to put in a kappa (κ) for a chi (χ or kh), and JJ may even have employed a sloppy χ. (Thanks to Benjamin Keim and Stephanie Nelson for the foregoing analysis of JJ’s Greek text.)
